For example, binder jetting offers a versatile range of materials for fabrication, and is currently being utilized for sand mold and casting applications (Wohlers, 2017).

Binder Jetting is defined as an "additive manufacturing process in which a liquid bonding agent is selectively deposited to join powder materials," according to ISO/ASTM 52900 (ASTM International, 2015).
A roller mechanism is utilized to spread the precursor powder onto a powder bed.
The powder particles are subsequently joined together through the deposition of binder, using a piezo-driven print head, according to a CAD design.

Microbial corrosion, or microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC), poses a significant threat to the durability of metals and alloys across various industries [47].
Sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB), a major contributor to MIC, are particularly prevalent in sectors such as oil and gas, marine, wastewater treatment, chemical processing, and energy production [812].
These industries often involve environments rich in water and nutrients that support SRB growth, leading to severe material degradation and safety risks.

These microorganisms can colonize and metabolize on metal surfaces and the intersection between microbial activity and the chemical environment surrounding steels can accelerate the corrosion rates, cause localized attack, and compromise the structural integrity severely [13,14].
As the global push for sustainability continues, designing materials that can withstand microbial threats while maintaining superior mechanical properties is a key challenge.

Open-source MD packages play a pivotal role in the development of algorithms and their practical applications.
GPUMD has many distinguishing features making it appealing to both users and developers.
Although the first version of GPUMD was released in 2017,[6] its development dates back to 2011 when it began as an exercise for a CUDA programming course.
It contains about 85,000 lines of source code written in CUDA C++.
For simplicity, we will use GPUMD to refer to GPUMD 4.0 unless otherwise stated.

Notably, at high scratching speeds, particularly at 100 m/s, the temperature softening effect dominates, reducing the activation energy required for dislocation movement [39], thus revitalizing the material's plastic deformation coordination and weakening the chip-breaking ability, resulting in large-sized serrated chips.
The body-centered cubic and hexagonal close-packed structures have relatively fewer slip systems, making the materials more prone to embrittlement.
Together, these factors determine whether a material is suitable for UHSM.
Material embrittlement in UHSM significantly alters heat generation and transfer [44].

As depicted in Fig. 18, in machining of metallic materials, approximately 75 %, 20 %, and 5 % of heat generation originates from internal friction in the primary deformation zone and external friction in the secondary and tertiary deformation zones, respectively.

As the machining speed increases, chips gradually transition from continuous to serrated types, indicating intensified adiabatic shearing and increased heat generation in the primary deformation zone.

Moreover, chips evolve from large serrated to small irregular fragmented types, significantly reducing their contact area with the tool and effectively diminishing heat from friction in the secondary deformation zone.

Moreover, reducing plastic deformation significantly lowers heat generation, and the extremely short contact time between the tool and the workpiece further restricts heat transfer deep into the workpiece, localizing subsurface damage to the shallow layers and presenting the skin effect of machining damage.
